title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 103)
hook: he knows our frame; he remembers we are dust

segments.voice: Yesterday, fields and trees joining the singing. Your line was a new song. Did your voice try something it had never done? Day four hundred thirty-one.

Memory is strangely lopsided. A teacher's sharp comment in seventh grade: still there, word for word, decades later. The stranger who held a door when your arms were full of groceries last Tuesday: gone by Wednesday. We keep the wounds on file and let the kindnesses slip through. It isn't a moral failing exactly. Memory seems to keep watch for threats. But left alone, it can make a life look harder and lonelier than it was. Psalm one hundred three knows this. It opens with a person giving their own soul a firm reminder, almost a nudge in the ribs. Don't forget.
screen: `THE SHARP COMMENT: KEPT.` → `THE HELD DOOR: FORGOTTEN.` → `A NUDGE TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred three begins, in the King James Bible: "Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." Like the deer psalm, the writer is talking to himself. But this time it isn't comfort. It's a reminder. Don't forget. Then he counts the benefits out loud, one after another: who forgives, who heals, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with lovingkindness, who renews your youth like the eagle's. Notice something about this psalm. It doesn't ask for anything. No request, no complaint, from beginning to end. It just remembers. Then come lines of great tenderness. "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." East and west never meet; you can travel east forever. "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust." Frame is how we're put together, what we're made of. God knows we're breakable, the psalm says, and is gentle about it. Our days are like grass, the wind passes over, and the place forgets us. And then the turn: "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting." We forget. God remembers that we're dust, and remembers mercy. By the end the psalm calls on the angels, every work of God, and finally its own soul again. Henry Francis Lyte turned it into a hymn, Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven, and churches still sing it.
screen: `TALKING TO YOUR OWN SOUL` · `COUNTING THE BENEFITS` · `AS FAR AS EAST FROM WEST` · `HE KNOWS WE ARE DUST` · then, large: `FORGET NOT ALL HIS BENEFITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list three benefits you've received. Not big abstract ones. Specific. A meal someone cooked. A body that got you out of bed. A friend who texted back. A bill that got paid. Take your time and find three. Say each one quietly, the way the psalm does: who gave me this, who gave me that. Then sit with the list. If you pray, you can say the line: bless the Lord, O my soul. If you don't, let the three things sit there, remembered on purpose. The bell holds the time.
Bless the Lord. Psalm one hundred three's opening, spoken to the writer's own soul: a reminder to praise, and not to forget.
Your line: forget not all his benefits. Today, when a small kindness comes your way, stop for one breath and file it on purpose, the way you'd file a hurt. Day four hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 103 as a prayer of thanksgiving, and it is sung in hymns such as Henry Francis Lyte's "Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven."

myth: Psalm 103 is full of requests to God
it asks for nothing. it remembers, from start to finish.
the psalm says God remembers we are dust
"for he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust."

fork.setup: you've just told your soul to bless the Lord. what does the psalm do next?
options: ask for a long list of things.
count, one by one, what has already been given.
fork.reveal: it lists the benefits: who forgiveth, who healeth, who redeemeth, who crowneth. the whole psalm asks for nothing.

original.note: Hebrew: bless, my soul. the psalm's opening command, spoken to the writer's own self.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful line from a worship song.
what it means: a person reminding their own soul to remember every good thing, because souls forget.
what a scholar hears: a psalm with no petitions at all, which opens and closes with the same words to the soul.

notes: Claim that Psalm 103 contains no petition. Confirm (it is commonly described as pure praise/thanksgiving).
Psalm 103 opens and closes with 'Bless the LORD, O my soul' (vv. 1, 22). Confirm.
Lyte, 'Praise, my soul, the King of heaven' (1834). Confirm date.
The hook's remark that minds attend more to threats than kindnesses is a general observation, not a scientific claim.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'most of us remember our lives as harder' (told the listener what they believe), the superlative 'some of the tenderest lines in the Bible', Lyte's 1834 date and 'many churches'.
